implementation_notes: Ruby's core classes expose the balking twin of each blocking operation: Mutex#try_lock 'returns immediately' with true/false instead of suspending the thread, and SizedQueue#push (aliases enq and <<) raises ThreadError when the queue is full if non_block is set. There are no synchronized methods, so the guarded-method structure is written by hand around those primitives, and the check and the state transition must share one Mutex region because the GVL does not make check-then-act atomic across thread switches. The blocking forms (Mutex#synchronize, plain Queue#pop) are the Guarded Suspension counterpart when a caller must eventually proceed.
pitfalls: Mutex#try_lock is not reentrant: a nested call balks even though the same thread holds the lock, so recursive guarded methods need an explicit owner check.
The state transition must sit inside the try_lock region - checking @state before taking the lock is a check-then-act race even under the GVL.
SizedQueue#push with non_block signals refusal by raising ThreadError ('queue full'); a broad rescue hides dropped work, so rescue ThreadError explicitly or prefer Mutex#try_lock's return value.
